title: Variation of Mass with Velocity in Special Relativity
short_intro: According to the special theory of relativity, the mass of an object depends on its relative speed with respect to an observer. The relativistic mass increases without bound as the velocity of the object approaches the speed of light in a vacuum.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of relativistic mass increase, energy-mass equivalence relation, and basic high-velocity particle behavior.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Rigorous derivation of relativistic mass variation using Lorentz transformations, momentum conservation in inelastic collisions, and transverse versus longitudinal mass formulations.

prerequisites: Postulates of Special Theory of Relativity
Lorentz transformations for space and time
Conservation of momentum and energy in mechanics

concept_notes.heading: Concept of Rest Mass versus Relativistic Mass
bullets: Rest mass (m_0) is the invariant mass of an object measured in the frame of reference where the object is at rest.
Relativistic mass (m) is the effective mass of a moving object as measured by an observer in a frame relative to which the object moves with velocity v.
The relation is given by m = m_0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2), where c is the speed of light.

concept_notes.heading: Behavior at Extreme Velocities
bullets: For speeds much smaller than c (v << c), the relativistic mass reduces to the classical Newtonian mass (m ≈ m_0).
As the velocity v approaches c, the denominator approaches zero, causing the relativistic mass to approach infinity.
Because an infinite force and energy would be required to accelerate a massive object to the speed of light, material particles can never reach or exceed c.

concept_notes.heading: Transverse and Longitudinal Mass
bullets: In advanced relativistic dynamics, force and acceleration are not necessarily collinear.
Longitudinal mass (m_L = m_0 / (1 - v^2/c^2)^(3/2)) governs acceleration parallel to the velocity vector.
Transverse mass (m_T = m_0 / (1 - v^2/c^2)^(1/2)) governs acceleration perpendicular to the velocity vector.

concept_notes.heading: Equivalence of Mass and Energy
bullets: The total relativistic energy of a free particle is expressed as E = mc^2.
The kinetic energy (K) is the difference between total energy and rest energy: K = (m - m_0)c^2.
In high-energy particle accelerators, increase in input energy manifests primarily as an increase in relativistic mass rather than classical velocity increments.

derivations.title: Derivation of Relativistic Mass Variation
derivations.conditions: Using conservation of linear momentum in two reference frames during a symmetric elastic-plastic collision.
steps: Consider two identical bodies A and B moving with equal and opposite velocities u_y and -u_y along the y-axis in frame S', and frame S moving with velocity v along the x-axis.
Body A is thrown from S' and body B from S such that they collide perfectly inelastically at the origin of S and come to rest together in S.
Using velocity addition formulas for the y-component of velocity in frame S: u_{y} = u'_{y} sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).
Applying conservation of momentum in frame S: m_A u_{yA} + m_B u_{yB} = (m_A + m_B) u_{yfinal}.
Solving for mass as a function of velocity yields m(v) = m_0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).

derivations.title: Derivation of Relativistic Kinetic Energy
derivations.conditions: Work-energy theorem applied under relativistic mechanics.
steps: Work done W to increase velocity from 0 to v is equal to change in kinetic energy: K = int F dx = int  rac{d(mv)}{dt} dx = int v d(mv).
Substitute m = m_0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) and integrate by parts.
K = int_{0}^{v} v dleft( rac{m_0 v}{sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}}ight).
Evaluation of the integral gives K =  rac{m_0 c^2}{sqrt{1 - v^2/c^2}} - m_0 c^2.
Expressing in terms of relativistic mass: K = mc^2 - m_0 c^2 = E - E_0.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Mass versus Velocity Curve
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of relativistic mass (m/m_0) on the y-axis against normalized velocity (v/c) on the x-axis, starting at (0, 1) and asymptotically shooting up to infinity as v/c approaches 1.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Shows that mass remains virtually constant at low speeds (Newtonian plateau) and increases sharply as speed approaches the speed of light.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently tested in TGT/PGT conceptual MCQs regarding asymptotic behavior at v = c.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Kaufmann-Bucherer-Neumann Experiments
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Experimental setup schematic showing deflection of beta particles (electrons) from radioactive sources in crossed electric and magnetic fields.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Confirmed that the charge-to-mass ratio (e/m) decreases with velocity exactly as predicted by the relativistic mass formula, validating Lorentz-Einstein mass variation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Historical and conceptual reference in PGT exams for experimental backing of relativistic mechanics.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Particle Accelerator Energy vs Velocity Limit
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A graph of particle velocity versus injected kinetic energy, showing velocity saturating at c despite continuous input of immense energy.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that added energy increases the relativistic mass rather than increasing the particle's speed once v is close to c.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Applied numerical and conceptual understanding of high-energy physics.

solved_numericals.question: At what fraction of the speed of light must a particle move so that its relativistic mass is twice its rest mass?
solution_steps: Use the mass-velocity relation: m = m_0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).
Substitute m: 2m_0 = m_0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) => 2 = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).

solved_numericals.question: Calculate the kinetic energy of an electron (rest mass m_0 = 9.1 	imes 10^{-31} kg) moving with a velocity of 0.6c. Express the answer in Joules and electron-volts (eV). (Take c = 3 	imes 10^8 m/s)
solution_steps: Identify rest mass m_0 = 9.1 	imes 10^{-31} kg and v = 0.6c.
Calculate the Lorentz factor gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - (0.6c/c)^2) = 1 / sqrt(1 - 0.36) = 1 / sqrt(0.64) = 1 / 0.8 = 1.25.
Use kinetic energy formula: K = (gamma - 1)m_0 c^2.
Substitute values: K = (1.25 - 1)(9.1 	imes 10^{-31})(3 	imes 10^8)^2 = 0.25 	imes (9.1 	imes 10^{-31}) 	imes (9 	imes 10^{16}).
Calculate Joules: K = 0.25 	imes 8.19 	imes 10^{-14} = 2.0475 	imes 10^{-14} J.
Convert to eV by dividing by electronic charge e = 1.6 	imes 10^{-19} C: K = (2.0475 	imes 10^{-14}) / (1.6 	imes 10^{-19}) = 1.28 	imes 10^{5} eV = 128 keV.

solved_numericals.question: Find the momentum of a proton whose kinetic energy is equal to its rest mass energy. (Rest mass of proton = m_0, speed of light = c)
solution_steps: Given condition: Kinetic Energy K = E_0 = m_0 c^2.
Total relativistic energy E = K + E_0 = m_0 c^2 + m_0 c^2 = 2m_0 c^2.
Use the energy-momentum relation: E^2 = p^2 c^2 + (m_0 c^2)^2.
Substitute E: (2m_0 c^2)^2 = p^2 c^2 + (m_0 c^2)^2.
Solve for momentum p: p^2 = 3 (m_0 c)^2 => p = sqrt{3} m_0 c.

assumptions_and_limitations: Special relativity assumes inertial frames of reference moving at constant relative velocities in the absence of strong gravitational fields.

The concept of 'relativistic mass' is mathematically valid and useful in dynamics, though modern theoretical physics frequently prefers keeping mass strictly as the invariant rest mass (m_0) and expressing velocity dependence entirely through momentum and energy.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An object's rest mass increases when it moves fast.
common_misconceptions.correct: Rest mass is an invariant scalar property; only the relativistic mass (or measured inertia) increases with velocity.
common_misconceptions.why: Rest mass is measured in the object's proper frame where v = 0, hence it remains constant regardless of the observer's frame.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Objects can exceed the speed of light if given infinite energy.
common_misconceptions.correct: As v approaches c, the relativistic mass and required energy approach infinity, making it impossible for massive particles to reach or exceed c.
common_misconceptions.why: The denominator sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2) tends to zero, creating an insurmountable asymptotic barrier.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Mass and weight are the same thing in relativistic transformations.
common_misconceptions.correct: Mass is an intrinsic measure of inertia, whereas weight depends on gravitational acceleration and metric properties in general relativity.
common_misconceptions.why: Relativity alters inertial mass with velocity, while gravitational mass behavior requires general relativistic treatments.

quick_revision: Relativistic mass increases with velocity according to m = m_0 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).
Total energy E = mc^2, rest energy E_0 = m_0 c^2, and kinetic energy K = (m - m_0)c^2.
Momentum is given by p = mv = m_0 v / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).
The energy-momentum invariant relation is E^2 = p^2 c^2 + (m_0 c^2)^2.
A massive particle can never attain the speed of light because its mass and required energy would become infinite.
